sections.title: Positions, semantics, and the scope of realism
Corroboration, intuition, and prima facie justification
Deep disagreement and the Zorpian comparison
Primitive concepts, circular definitions, and practical force
Explanatory parsimony and the genealogy of moral belief

routes.speaker: Eric Sampson
routes.position: Non-naturalist moral realism is true: some moral beliefs are stance-independently true and concern irreducible normative properties.

bridges.statement: Clear moral cases justify belief that stance-independent normative truths exist.
Stance-independent reasons are intelligible considerations favoring action regardless of an agent's goals.
Strong undefeated intuitions about paradigm cases provide prima facie justification for moral realism.
Non-natural moral facts need not satisfy empirical detection, prediction, or reductive-definition tests.
Realism explains genuine normative facts that a purely psychological account leaves out.

routes.speaker: Lance Bush
routes.position: Moral realism is unjustified or unintelligible because normativity is relational and moral-realist concepts lack independent explanatory content.

bridges.statement: There are no warranted stance-independent moral facts, and realist accounts are unintelligible, false, or trivial.
Reasons and evaluative claims are intelligible only relative to goals, standards, attitudes, or consistency relations.
Realist intuitions lack a public standard capable of adjudicating fundamental normative disagreement.
Moral-realist belief is better explained through psychological projection and culturally contingent genealogy.
Ordinary moral discourse is metaethically plural and indeterminate rather than uniformly realist.
